paragraphs: Learning several related models creates an opportunity to encourage sparsity jointly. Instead of merely making each model use few parameters, joint regularization encourages a coordinated sparse solution across the collection. This paper develops an optimization method for the L1,Infinity norm, which extends the sparse modeling role of L1 regularization to this shared setting.

The proposed method uses projected gradient optimization. Its central computational requirement is an efficient way to project parameter values onto an L1,Infinity ball, bringing an update back into the permitted region. The paper supplies an algorithm for this operation that takes O(n log n) time and O(n) memory, where n counts the parameters. This addresses the main obstacle to using the projected gradient approach.

The authors evaluate the method on multi-task image annotation. In that experiment, L1,Infinity regularization performs better than both L2 and L1 regularization and discovers jointly sparse solutions. These findings support the practical value of coordinating sparsity across related prediction tasks, alongside the contribution of an efficient optimization building block.
icml-2009-an-efficient-projection-for-l1.tldr: An efficient projection algorithm makes joint sparse regularization practical and improves performance in a multi-task image annotation experiment.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning fits a rule for measuring how far apart examples are. In a high-dimensional space, that rule can become complex, especially when relatively few examples are available. This paper introduces a sparse metric learning formulation that uses an L1 penalty together with log-determinant regularization to control the complexity of the learned distance model.

The approach explicitly uses an assumption of sparsity in the underlying feature relationships. Through an analogy with covariance estimation, the authors establish a consistency result for a target distance matrix with at most m nonzero entries per row. The stated convergence rate is O(sqrt((m² log d)/n)). Its dependence on sparsity and dimension makes the structural assumption central to the theoretical result.

For computation, the formulation supports block coordinate descent, which updates portions of the optimization variables in turn. The authors report that this is much faster than standard semidefinite programming approaches used for metric learning. Comparisons on several datasets yield competitive results, supporting the combination of sparse modeling and more efficient optimization.
icml-2009-an-efficient-sparse-metric-lea.tldr: Sparse metric learning combines L1 and log-determinant regularization with efficient optimization and a consistency result for sparse target matrices.

paragraphs: A recursive algorithm can often be implemented in many different ways, with different execution speeds. This paper studies how to choose fast implementations when the possibilities can be described by a grammar, including algorithms such as fast Fourier transforms. The challenge is to search this structured collection without spending excessive time evaluating alternatives.

The proposed algorithm reformulates the task as maximizing an objective over the terminal nodes, or sinks, of a directed acyclic graph. It estimates node values through Monte Carlo sampling and expands a subgraph toward promising choices. Local multi-armed bandit problems guide this expansion, connecting decisions about where to search with sampled evidence about implementation quality.

Inside an adaptive linear transform library, the method reduces search time by an order of magnitude compared with the existing algorithm. In some cases, the resulting implementations also perform up to 10% better. The two benefits are distinct: faster tuning reduces the effort needed to choose an implementation, while faster implementations can improve applications that use the library.
icml-2009-bandit-based-optimization-on-g.tldr: A graph search guided by sampling and bandit decisions substantially reduces library tuning time and sometimes finds faster implementations.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning methods assume that an agent chooses from a small set of discrete actions, while control problems often require continuously valued actions. A common workaround divides the action range into coarse choices. Binary Action Search offers a way to use discrete-action learning methods while searching a continuous action range at arbitrarily fine resolution.

The method builds an internal binary policy over an augmented state space. This policy chooses increments or decrements to action variables, and those decisions search for the action to execute. The abstract states that the approach can be combined with any discrete-action reinforcement learning algorithm. It also removes the restrictive modification steps of Adaptive Action Modification and does not require temporal action locality.

The authors combine Binary Action Search with Least-Squares Policy Iteration and Fitted Q-Iteration. They investigate it on the Inverted Pendulum, Double Integrator, and Car on the Hill domains, each involving continuous states and actions. These demonstrations examine a general interface between discrete decision algorithms and continuous control, with resolution handled through the internal search.
icml-2009-binary-action-search-for-learn.tldr: Binary Action Search uses internal increment-or-decrement decisions to let discrete-action reinforcement learning algorithms learn continuous-action policies.

paragraphs: Approximate linear programming is a reinforcement learning technique with attractive theoretical properties, yet its practical solutions can be poor. This paper investigates that gap in problems where the approximation creates virtual loops. Identifying this source of difficulty motivates changes to the optimization constraints that determine the resulting solution.

The authors propose two approaches. The first rolls out selected constraints, using information from the dual optimization problem to guide which constraints receive this treatment. The second relaxes the approximate linear program through external penalty methods. This provides an alternative for domains where rolling out constraints is impractical, so the two methods address different computational circumstances.

Both approaches produce promising empirical results on simple benchmark problems and on a more realistic blood inventory management problem. The findings connect a diagnosis of approximation-related trouble with concrete ways to improve solution quality. Their significance is practical: modifying how constraints are handled can help address weaknesses in approximate linear programming, including settings where the rollout-based remedy cannot readily be applied.
icml-2009-constraint-relaxation-in-appro.tldr: Two constraint-handling methods address poor approximate linear programming solutions associated with virtual loops and show promising empirical results.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational cost of variational Bayesian inference for very large generalized linear models. The authors introduce a relaxation of the inference problem and prove that it is convex whenever the model is log-concave. That condition specifies the scope of the convexity guarantee and gives the approximation a useful optimization structure.

They provide a general double-loop algorithm for models with arbitrary super-Gaussian potentials. The algorithm repeatedly separates coupled parts of the objective, allowing most computation to be performed by solving large linear systems. This reformulation is the central efficiency mechanism: it turns much of the inference workload into a recurring type of numerical problem.

The authors report speed improvements of orders of magnitude over previously proposed solvers for the same problem. They evaluate the method through Bayesian active learning with large binary classification models, including settings with many candidates and sequential inclusion steps. The work therefore links an optimization guarantee under a stated model condition with a computational strategy for demanding inference and selection tasks.
icml-2009-convex-variational-bayesian-in.tldr: A variational inference relaxation is convex for log-concave models and admits a solver that shifts most computation to large linear systems.

paragraphs: Unlabeled video contains a useful relationship between observations: neighboring frames are likely to show the same objects. This paper proposes a learning method for deep architectures that uses this temporal coherence as a source of supervision. The sequence itself supplies information about related observations, even though the frames have no supplied object labels.

The key idea is to use continuity over time to support a supervised task of interest. Images of an object may vary across successive frames while still depicting that object. Treating nearby frames as related therefore provides a learning signal relevant to recognizing objects despite changes in appearance. The relationship is probabilistic: successive frames are likely to share objects, rather than guaranteed to do so.

The authors demonstrate the method on some object and face recognition tasks requiring robustness to pose. Their reported effectiveness supports using sequential relationships in unlabeled recordings to improve supervised recognition. The contribution centers on how training information is obtained: temporal structure becomes a usable signal for learning deep representations.
icml-2009-deep-learning-from-temporal-co.tldr: Temporal continuity in unlabeled video supplies a training signal that improves performance on some pose-invariant object and face recognition tasks.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether the true direction of a time series can be recovered from its observations. The method fits an autoregressive moving average model and examines the relationship between noise and earlier samples. If noise is independent of previous samples in one ordering but dependent in the reverse ordering, it chooses the former.

The authors prove that the method works at the population level under their process model when the noise is not normally distributed. With normally distributed noise, the direction is not identifiable. This result supports a causal reasoning principle in the time-series setting: an asymmetry in noise independence after regression can distinguish the true direction from its reverse.

Experiments use simulated data conforming to the modeling assumptions and real EEG recordings. The method makes decisions for a significant fraction of both collections, and those decisions are mostly correct. On the real data it outperforms alternative time-direction recovery methods. The empirical claim thus concerns the decisions actually made, alongside a theoretical guarantee with explicit distributional conditions.
icml-2009-detecting-the-direction-of-cau.tldr: Noise-independence asymmetry can recover time-series direction, with a population guarantee for non-normal noise and mostly correct decisions in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Topics in a document collection can be correlated, and understanding those relationships is part of modeling the text. Independent Factor Topic Models extend the Correlated Topic Model by introducing linear latent variable models for the hidden sources of topic correlation. These sources provide an additional level of explanation for why topics vary together.

A sparse prior over the sources makes sparse patterns of topic relationships directly visualizable. The source variables also imply a conditional independence assumption that lets the objective separate into factors. The authors use this structure to develop a fast variational inference algorithm based on Newton-Raphson optimization. Thus, the latent-source formulation serves both interpretation and computation.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show average runtimes three to five times faster than the Correlated Topic Model, while maintaining competitive held-out perplexity and log-likelihood. The reported benefit is a substantial speed improvement alongside competitive predictive performance. The model also offers a way to inspect the sparse sources underlying topic correlations, connecting efficiency with a more interpretable representation.
icml-2009-independent-factor-topic-model.tldr: Independent Factor Topic Models expose sparse sources of topic correlation and run three to five times faster on average than CTM in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Comparing two clusterings requires a measure of how similarly they group the same data. This paper examines information-theoretic similarity measures and asks how much of their score can arise by chance. The authors observe that the average score under random partitioning is not constant, complicating the interpretation of an unadjusted similarity value.

This baseline varies more when the number of data points is small relative to the number of clusters. The issue also occurs in some measures outside the information-theoretic family, including the Rand Index. A score can therefore reflect features of the partitioning setup as well as meaningful agreement between the clusterings.

Assuming a hypergeometric model of randomness, the authors derive an analytical expression for expected mutual information. They use it to construct adjusted versions of several popular information-theoretic measures and provide examples showing their usefulness. The correction gives similarity scores a chance-based reference under the specified random model, helping separate observed agreement from the agreement that model would already predict.
icml-2009-information-theoretic-measures.tldr: Chance agreement can distort clustering similarity scores, motivating adjusted information-theoretic measures based on expected mutual information.

paragraphs: Unsupervised learning can use large quantities of unlabeled data, but training time can restrict both model size and the number of examples processed. This paper tackles that computational bottleneck for deep belief networks and sparse coding. It develops general principles for distributing their learning computations across the massive parallelism available in graphics processors.

For deep belief networks, the authors report an implementation up to 55 times faster than a dual-core CPU implementation. One example trains a four-layer network with 100 million free parameters in around a day, reducing a workload that otherwise takes several weeks. This illustrates how faster computation can make substantially larger training jobs practical.

For sparse coding, the paper introduces a simple algorithm designed to be inherently parallel and reports speedups of five to sixteen times over previous methods. Together, the results demonstrate successful scaling for two different unsupervised learning approaches. The contribution combines hardware-oriented computation principles with algorithm design, showing that both can help remove training-time barriers to large models.
icml-2009-large-scale-deep-unsupervised-.tldr: GPU parallelization substantially accelerates deep belief network and sparse coding training, enabling larger unsupervised learning workloads.

paragraphs: Complex movements can often be described as sequences of simpler movements. Drawing a triangle, for example, has recognizable component steps. This paper uses that observation to motivate temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning for motor skills: a learner can make decisions about motion templates that represent more extended pieces of behavior.

The authors argue that selecting forces or torques at a very fast timescale makes learning unnecessarily difficult. It complicates both the policy and temporal credit assignment, the problem of determining which earlier decisions contributed to an outcome. Organizing behavior around simpler motion templates changes the scale at which those decisions are made.

The paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework built around these templates and presents an algorithm that can learn high-quality policies using only a few abstract decisions. The stated benefit is a reduction in decision complexity through meaningful movement units. This connects the decomposition of a long motor task with a learning procedure that sequences its simpler components.
icml-2009-learning-complex-motions-by-se.tldr: A reinforcement learning framework sequences motion templates to learn high-quality motor policies with few abstract decisions.

paragraphs: Undirected graphical models represent statistical dependencies without assigning a direction to every connection. They can be a natural fit for real-world domains, but learning their structure with likelihood-based scores is difficult. The obstacle highlighted here is the partition function, whose computation can be intractable and thereby complicate comparisons between candidate structures.

The paper introduces a structure learning algorithm for Markov random fields, motivated by canonical parameterization. Its computational improvement is to learn canonical factors for individual variables. This change makes the algorithm suitable for domains with hundreds of nodes, bringing the representation strategy into a more substantial problem scale.

The authors compare the method with algorithms for both directed and undirected models using simulated data and real biological datasets. It frequently produces higher-quality structures than existing algorithms. These results suggest that enforcing consistency during structure learning is beneficial for undirected graphs. The empirical conclusion is qualified by its frequency across the comparisons, while the main methodological contribution is a more computationally practical factor-learning approach.
icml-2009-learning-structurally-consiste.tldr: Learning per-variable canonical factors enables structure learning for undirected models with hundreds of nodes and frequently improves structural quality in experiments.

paragraphs: An anytime algorithm can return an answer at essentially any point, with answer quality typically improving as it runs longer. This creates a decision about computation itself: when is the current answer good enough to stop? The paper studies learning that stopping decision across a sequence of independent, identically distributed tasks.

The objective is expected average reward per unit time. It therefore evaluates the benefit of better answers together with the time spent obtaining them. The proposed algorithm combines the Cross Entropy method for global optimization with local gradient ascent, using both broad search and local improvement to learn when computation should end.

The authors also theoretically investigate how far their estimated gradient can be from the true gradient. Empirical demonstrations include a toy problem and a real-world face detection task. These results support the applicability of learning a stopping policy, while the formulation makes the central tradeoff explicit: additional computation is useful according to how it contributes to reward relative to elapsed time.
icml-2009-learning-when-to-stop-thinking.tldr: A learned stopping policy balances answer quality against computation time to optimize expected reward per unit time across repeated tasks.

paragraphs: Semantic image segmentation assigns class labels to local regions of an image. A region's own appearance provides useful evidence, while information about the image as a whole can also inform its label. This paper combines those two information sources through a conditional random field and a separate image classification method.

The image is first divided into patches through unsupervised pre-segmentation at multiple scales. Patch labels become the variables in the conditional random field, which is coupled to local image features. The image classifier considers global features, and its output constrains the conditional random field. This gives whole-image information an explicit role in determining local segment labels.

The authors demonstrate and compare the approach on a standard semantic segmentation dataset. The contribution described in the abstract is the integration mechanism: local structured labeling operates under constraints supplied by global classification. This design addresses the problem of combining evidence available at different spatial scopes within a single segmentation procedure.
icml-2009-multi-class-image-segmentation.tldr: A global image classifier constrains a patch-based conditional random field to combine whole-image context with local evidence for semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor methods depend on which data points appear close to others. This paper examines a property of that relationship called k-occurrence: how many times a point appears among the k nearest neighbors of other points. Counting these appearances reveals how unevenly the dataset distributes the role of being a neighbor.

The authors show that this distribution becomes considerably more skewed as dimensionality increases. Some points appear in many other points' neighbor lists and become hubs. The paper investigates the origin of this behavior and identifies it as an inherent property of high-dimensional vector space, adding another aspect to the difficulties associated with high dimensionality.

The work also explores what hub formation means for classification, clustering, and information retrieval, all of which can rely on vector-space distances. Its contribution is to draw attention to the distribution of neighbor appearances across a dataset. Understanding that distribution helps characterize how high-dimensional geometry shapes the relationships used by these applications.
icml-2009-nearest-neighbors-in-high-dime.tldr: High-dimensional data develops hubs that occur unusually often in nearest-neighbor lists, with implications for distance-based learning and retrieval.

paragraphs: Factor analysis explains observations through combinations of underlying factors. This paper proposes a Bayesian nonparametric extension using a beta process prior, called beta process factor analysis. The model decomposes data into linear combinations of a sparse set of factors, providing a representation of structure underlying the observed measurements.

Sparsity is central to that representation: the decomposition emphasizes a limited set of contributing factors. The beta process supplies the Bayesian prior underlying the extension. The authors highlight its conjugacy, which supports analytical posterior calculations and straightforward inference. This connects the modeling choice to the practical problem of learning the hidden factor structure from data.

The paper derives a variational Bayes inference algorithm and demonstrates the model on MNIST handwritten digits and the HGDP-CEPH cell line panel. These applications show the proposed factor representation being used with two different datasets. The contribution combines a sparse nonparametric model with an explicit inference procedure, making the proposed decomposition something that can be fitted to observations.
icml-2009-nonparametric-factor-analysis-.tldr: Beta process factor analysis provides a Bayesian nonparametric model for sparse linear factor decompositions, with variational inference and dataset demonstrations.

paragraphs: Similarity judgments need not specify exact numerical distances between objects. They can instead say that one pair should be closer than another. This paper studies embedding objects such as images, audio, and documents into Euclidean space while respecting a partial ordering of pairwise distances, a form of information that arises naturally in modeling human similarity perception.

Representing the constraints as a partial order allows the method to use graph-theoretic tools. The authors use this structure to produce embeddings more efficiently and to exploit relationships across the full constraint collection. The approach therefore treats the ordering information as a structured whole when constructing the space.

The proposed embedding algorithm is based on semidefinite programming and can be parameterized with multiple kernels. This allows heterogeneous features to contribute to a unified representation. The resulting framework links relative similarity constraints with a way to combine different descriptions of the objects, so both the supplied ordering and the available feature sources can shape the embedding.
icml-2009-partial-order-embedding-with-m.tldr: A semidefinite embedding method uses partial orders of distances and multiple kernels to combine similarity constraints with heterogeneous features.

paragraphs: This paper proposes regression that minimizes statistical dependence between the input variables and the residuals left after prediction. The motivation comes from causal inference with additive noise models, where the relationship between inputs and unexplained variation matters. The method does not assume a particular noise distribution, making it nonparametric with respect to that distribution.

The authors argue that this objective suits causal inference, but identify a practical difficulty: optimization is generally nonconvex and can be hard to solve. Despite that obstacle, they report good results on a causality challenge task involving pairs of statistically dependent variables. The task is to distinguish which variable is the cause and which is the effect.

The paper also proposes an efficient algorithm for inferring causal models from observational data with more than two variables. Its required number of regressions and independence tests grows quadratically with the number of variables. This improves on the simple strategy of testing every possible directed acyclic graph, connecting the regression criterion with a more scalable causal-model search.
icml-2009-regression-by-dependence-minim.tldr: Dependence-minimizing regression supports additive-noise causal inference without specifying a noise distribution, though its optimization is generally nonconvex.

paragraphs: An optimization procedure returns a solution, but understanding how that solution responds to changes in the problem is a separate question. This paper introduces a method for quantifying solution stability across a large class of combinatorial optimization problems in machine learning. Its development is strongly motivated by linear programming relaxations.

The authors apply the method to correlation clustering, clustering aggregation, modularity clustering, and relative performance significance clustering. They prove that when a relaxation is used to solve the original clustering problem, their calculated stability is conservative. Specifically, it never overestimates the stability of the original, unrelaxed problem, giving the estimate a clear direction of reliability.

The method can also compute the entire sequence of optimal solutions as the optimization problem is increasingly perturbed. This describes how solutions change beyond a single stability assessment. Experiments show good performance on several benchmark problems. Together, these contributions provide both a conservative stability measure and a way to follow changes in the optimizer under growing perturbations.
icml-2009-solution-stability-in-linear-p.tldr: A relaxation-based method conservatively measures clustering solution stability and can trace optimal solutions as perturbations increase.

paragraphs: Sequence labeling can benefit from features involving larger patterns of labels, but training data often provides insufficient evidence for many such higher-order features. This paper starts from the observation that only a small number are useful. Sparse Higher Order Conditional Random Fields combine local features with a sparse collection of higher-order features.

The central computational insight is to group states and transitions that share the same potential functions. Exact inference then operates on those groups. This exploits shared structure in the model's scoring functions and supports practical efficiency when higher-order features are sparse. The authors explicitly note that the complexity is still not polynomial.

Experiments cover optical character recognition and Chinese organization name recognition. Using the same higher-order feature set, the proposed models significantly outperform previous approaches. These results show the value of the inference formulation in the tested tasks: sparse higher-order information can be incorporated alongside local information without giving up exact inference, even though the general computational complexity remains nonpolynomial.
icml-2009-sparse-higher-order-conditiona.tldr: Grouping equivalent states and transitions enables practically efficient exact inference for CRFs with sparse higher-order features.

paragraphs: Supervised learning becomes more complicated when several annotators provide labels and those labels may be noisy. This paper considers the setting where there is also no absolute gold standard to resolve disagreements. The available expert judgments must therefore support learning even though the actual labels are hidden and cannot simply be read from a trusted reference.

The proposed probabilistic approach addresses two linked questions: how to evaluate the different experts and how to estimate the underlying labels. Its algorithm produces both kinds of estimates. This makes the quality of the annotation sources part of the learning problem, alongside the task of deciding what labels the examples should receive.

Experiments indicate that the method clearly outperforms majority voting, a commonly used way to combine annotations. The result supports modeling the experts and hidden labels when learning from uncertain judgments. Its practical significance is that disagreement need not be resolved solely by counting votes; the proposed probabilistic treatment offers a tested alternative in the stated setting without a gold standard.
icml-2009-supervised-learning-from-multi.tldr: A probabilistic method jointly evaluates annotators and estimates hidden labels, outperforming majority voting in reported experiments without a gold standard.

paragraphs: Surrogate regret bounds relate performance under a surrogate loss to the regret of the prediction task it supports. This paper establishes tight bounds for proper losses, described in the abstract as Fisher consistent. The results generalize earlier margin-based bounds, extending the theoretical treatment to this class of losses.

The proof uses Taylor's theorem and produces new representations of both loss and regret. It also gives a simple proof of an integral representation for proper losses. These representations are part of the contribution because they provide mathematical ways to express the quantities involved in the bounds and clarify the structure of the loss family.

The authors additionally reformulate a duality result for Bregman divergences. From this, they demonstrate the convexity of composite losses constructed using canonical link functions. The paper thus connects guarantees about regret with the mathematical form of loss functions and their optimization properties. Its stated findings are theoretical, combining tight bounds, representation results, and a convexity demonstration.
icml-2009-surrogate-regret-bounds-for-pr.tldr: The paper derives tight regret bounds for proper losses and connects their representations to convexity under canonical link functions.

paragraphs: Group-Lasso estimators are useful in many applications, but the paper identifies a problem with uncertainty assessment: they lack meaningful variance estimates for regression coefficients. The authors propose a fully Bayesian treatment to address this issue. Their construction extends the standard Bayesian Lasso through a hierarchical expansion for the Group-Lasso setting.

The method is applied to Poisson models for contingency tables, which organize counts across categories. Inference uses an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. The Bayesian formulation brings coefficient uncertainty into the model, connecting the original motivation about variance estimates with a procedure for analyzing these count-based data.

Simulated experiments with known ground truth validate the method's performance on artificial datasets. An application to breast cancer data demonstrates its ability to identify differences in marker-protein interaction patterns between patient groups. That finding concerns statistical interaction patterns in the analyzed data. Together, the applications show how the Bayesian treatment can support both uncertainty-aware estimation and comparisons of relationships across groups.
icml-2009-the-bayesian-group-lasso-for-a.tldr: A Bayesian Group-Lasso formulation addresses coefficient uncertainty and identifies differing marker-protein interaction patterns in a breast cancer dataset.

paragraphs: Human locomotion combines shared movement structure with differences between activities or people. This paper learns a hierarchy of locomotion styles from unlabeled motion capture data by exploiting repeated movement cycles. Its aim is to identify both the common structure and the characteristics that distinguish individual styles.

The model assumes that cycles within one style are noisy, temporally warped versions of a single hidden cycle. Each style-specific cycle is drawn from a shared parent distribution representing structure common to the motions. This hierarchy links style differences with a common basis while explicitly accounting for variations in timing.

Learning jointly produces aligned latent cycle distributions, probabilities of style labels for each example, cycle segmentations, and temporal warps relative to the latent cycles. These outputs connect style discovery with the timing and segmentation needed to interpret the recordings. Demonstrations include style clustering, animation, style blending, and filling in missing data, illustrating the model's flexibility across several motion-related applications under its cyclic modeling assumptions.
icml-2009-unsupervised-hierarchical-mode.tldr: A hierarchical model discovers locomotion styles from unlabeled motion capture while jointly estimating cycles, timing variations, and style probabilities.
